passage: Day one: Amandeep, fifteen months, stands holding the sofa and reaches for a ball. He leans too far and thumps down on his bottom. Preeti, his mother, rolls the ball closer. A week later he bends to pick up the ball, wobbles, and slaps one hand on the floor to steady himself before rising. Two weeks on, he carries the ball across the rug, steps over Preeti's outstretched leg, sways, and stays upright.

qa.q: What did Amandeep step over in the last beat?
qa.a: Preeti's outstretched leg.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt when he leaned toward the ball?
qa.a: He seemed eager to reach the ball, keen enough to lean too far while still holding the sofa.

qa.q: How could Preeti give Amandeep more safe balance practice?
qa.a: She can place toys just out of reach on soft ground so he has to shift his weight, while staying near.

qa.q: What would change if the floor were hard tiles with no rug?
qa.a: Falls would hurt more, so Preeti might stay closer or add a mat, and Amandeep might be more cautious.

grounding: Shows a toddler gaining steadiness over weeks, from falling when leaning to catching himself and staying upright.

passage: On the big bed in their Kolkata flat, Anirban, two, stands on the soft mattress while his father Suraj folds laundry. Each time Suraj tugs a bedsheet, the mattress dips. Anirban bends his knees, sticks his arms out and sways like a boat, then grins. Once he tips sideways; his hand shoots out to the pillow and he doesn't fall. Suraj stops folding, moves the laundry basket off the edge, then pulls the next sheet more slowly.

qa.q: What does Suraj move off the edge of the bed?
qa.a: The laundry basket.

qa.q: What does Anirban's grin suggest about how he felt swaying?
qa.a: He seems to be enjoying the wobbly challenge rather than being scared.

qa.q: What did Suraj do that kept the game safer?
qa.a: He moved the basket away and pulled the sheet more slowly, so Anirban could keep practising with less risk.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel when Anirban's hand shoots out to the pillow?
qa.a: He might feel a flash of worry, then relief that Anirban caught himself.

grounding: Shows a toddler using core strength to stay upright on a shifting surface and catch himself.

passage:
"Hold my finger, Raghav. We'll walk on the little garden wall."
"Me! Me!"
"Okay, slow. Look, you're leaning."
"Oh-oh!"
"You caught yourself! Hand on my shoulder."
Mummy called from the gate, "Varun, stay right beside him, okay?"
"I am. Raghav, bend your knees a bit."
"Down!"
"Down? Or again?"
"Again!"
"Mummy, he did the whole wall and only wobbled twice!"
"I saw. Well done, both of you."

qa.q: How many times did Raghav wobble on the wall?
qa.a: Twice, according to Varun.

qa.q: What does Raghav's shout of "Again!" suggest he wanted?
qa.a: He enjoyed the walk and wanted to keep practising his balance.

qa.q: How is Varun supporting Raghav's balance, and what makes it work?
qa.a: He offers a finger and shoulder and simple tips like bending his knees, while letting Raghav do the walking himself.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Varun's role here?
qa.a: She trusts him to help but keeps watch, and seems proud of both boys. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler shifting weight and steadying himself while walking along a low wall.

passage:
Nursery note, Yash (caregiver), Tuesday.

Karthik, twenty months, walked along the chalk line on the floor today, arms out wide. When he turned, he wobbled but put one foot back and stayed up. Later he bent down to pick up a car and stood again without holding on. On the soft slope he fell sideways and caught himself with one hand. He looked surprised, then laughed. Next week I'll add a low beam with a mat underneath.

qa.q: What did Karthik walk along today?
qa.a: He walked along the chalk line on the floor, arms out wide.

qa.q: What does Karthik's laugh after falling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he wasn't upset by the fall and felt safe enough to enjoy it.

qa.q: How is Yash planning to support Karthik's balance?
qa.a: Yash plans to add a low beam with a mat underneath for safe practice.

qa.q: How might Karthik's parents see this note?
qa.a: They might feel pleased that Karthik is getting steadier and learning to catch himself.

grounding: Shows a caregiver noting a toddler's growing balance as he shifts weight and catches himself.

passage: In the mango orchard near their village, Salma, two, follows her aunt Deepika over bumpy ground. She wobbles over a root, sways, and plants both feet wide. She stops, steadies herself, and keeps going. When she bends to pick up a fallen leaf, she tips forward and puts a hand down. Deepika waits instead of lifting her. Salma pushes up, stands, and holds the leaf up high.

qa.q: What does Salma pick up in the orchard?
qa.a: She picks up a fallen leaf.

qa.q: How can you tell Salma feels proud when she stands up?
qa.a: She holds the leaf up high, like she's showing off what she did.

qa.q: How does Deepika's waiting help Salma learn to balance?
qa.a: She waits instead of lifting her, letting Salma catch herself and stand.

qa.q: What would change if Deepika always carried Salma over bumpy ground?
qa.a: Salma would get fewer chances to practise steadying herself on uneven ground.

grounding: Shows a toddler balancing on uneven ground and catching herself when she tips.

passage: Elif, two and a bit, wanted to walk the low wooden edge of the sandpit in the Berlin courtyard. Liam, the student who babysat her on Wednesdays, held out a finger. She waved it away. Three steps in, she tipped left, bent her knees, flung her arms out, and stayed up. On the corner she tipped again and this time dropped onto her bottom in the sand, then climbed straight back on.

qa.q: Where was the edge that Elif walked along?
qa.a: The low wooden edge of the sandpit in the Berlin courtyard.

qa.q: Why might Elif have waved Liam's finger away?
qa.a: She wanted to do it on her own and seemed confident enough to try without help.

qa.q: How could Liam support Elif on the sandpit edge without taking over?
qa.a: Stay close by, let her wobble and catch herself, and step in only if she is about to fall somewhere hard.

qa.q: What would change if the edge were next to concrete instead of sand?
qa.a: Liam would probably need to hold her hand, because a fall would hurt far more than dropping onto sand.

grounding: Shows a toddler shifting her weight on a narrow edge, catching herself with bent knees and arms, and recovering from a fall.

passage: I'm Afreen, and I watch my little cousin Hansa after school while her mother cooks. Yesterday Hansa was carrying her doll across the rug when her foot caught the edge. I thought she'd go flat on her face, but she threw one hand to the floor, bent low, and pushed herself back up without letting go of the doll. Later she squatted to pick up a crayon and stood again with no hands. I don't know if she was scared; she just kept walking.

qa.q: What was Hansa carrying across the rug?
qa.a: Her doll.

qa.q: What might Hansa have felt when her foot caught the rug?
qa.a: Maybe a quick fright, but she seemed calm and determined, since she caught herself and kept walking without crying.

qa.q: What could Afreen do to keep Hansa's practice safe at home?
qa.a: Keep the rug edges flat and the floor clear of sharp things, while still letting Hansa walk and squat freely.

qa.q: How does Afreen see what happened compared with what was expected?
qa.a: Afreen expected a hard fall, so it is a surprise that Hansa saved herself with one hand.

grounding: Shows a toddler catching herself mid-trip and squatting and standing without support, described by an older cousin.

passage: First day of the monsoon: Tejas, fourteen months, stood holding the window grille to watch the rain, and every time thunder cracked he sat down with a bump. His mother Rajni knelt beside him. Two weeks later: he stood watching without holding on, swaying as he turned to point at the puddles. The last week of the rains: he stepped from the doormat onto the wet verandah, slid, and caught himself on one knee before Rajni could reach him.

qa.q: What did Tejas hold while watching the rain on the first day?
qa.a: The window grille.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been feeling when he sat down at each thunder crack?
qa.a: He was probably startled or a little scared, and sitting down felt safer than standing.

qa.q: How could Rajni help Tejas practise balance during the rainy weeks?
qa.a: Let him stand and turn near the window while wiping the wet verandah floor, so his slips happen on safe ground.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni when Tejas slides on the verandah?
qa.a: It is probably a jolt of worry, followed by relief that he caught himself on one knee.

grounding: Shows a toddler's balance growing over the monsoon, from holding on to standing free to catching himself on a slip.

passage: On Holi morning, the colony courtyard in Jaipur was wet and pink. Arohi, twenty-two months, toddled after the bigger children, her white frock streaked green. Her foot slid on a puddle. She swayed, flung both arms out wide, bent her knees, and stayed up. Her mother, Anjali, one step behind, let out a breath and didn't pick her up. Arohi looked back at her, surprised at herself, then carried on, arms still out like wings.

qa.q: What was the courtyard like on Holi morning?
qa.a: Wet and pink.

qa.q: What did Arohi's look back at her mother suggest?
qa.a: Arohi seemed surprised and a little proud that she hadn't fallen.

qa.q: How did Anjali support Arohi's balance on the slippery courtyard?
qa.a: She stayed one step behind, close enough to help, but let Arohi catch herself instead of picking her up.

qa.q: What was it like for Anjali when Arohi slid?
qa.a: Anjali felt a moment of fear, then relief, choosing to trust Arohi's steadiness.

grounding: On a slippery Holi morning, a toddler catches her balance with arms and knees while her mother stays close.

passage:
"New boots, Uday! For the rain."
Uday, two, stood still, staring at his big yellow gumboots.
"Walk to Mamma?" Shreya crouched at the end of the verandah.
Uday took a heavy step. Clomp. He tipped sideways, grabbed the pillar, steadied himself.
"Hold on. Now let go."
"No."
"Okay. Hold on and walk."
Clomp, clomp. He let go of the pillar himself. Clomp. He wobbled, bent his knees, stayed up.
"Uday! You did it!"
"Again!" He turned, carefully, and clomped back.

qa.q: What colour were Uday's new gumboots?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt when he refused to let go of the pillar?
qa.a: Uday felt unsure and a bit nervous in the heavy new boots.

qa.q: How did Shreya help Uday build confidence in his balance?
qa.a: She accepted his 'no', let him hold on, and waited until he chose to let go himself.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel when Uday lets go by himself?
qa.a: Shreya would likely feel delighted and proud, seeing him gain confidence at his own pace.

grounding: At the start of the monsoon, a toddler learns to balance in heavy new gumboots with his mother's patient encouragement.

passage: Daycare note, the week before Christmas. Karthik (2) spent a long time on the balance beam we set up beside the paper-star decorations. It's only a plank on the floor. At first he walked it sideways, holding the wall. Today he walked it facing forward, arms out, and when he wobbled, he crouched low instead of falling. He did it four times. Next week I'll add a second plank at an angle, and I'll tell his parents. — Vikas

qa.q: What was the balance beam made of?
qa.a: A plank on the floor.

qa.q: What might Karthik have felt when he crouched instead of falling?
qa.a: Karthik was probably a little startled but steady, and pleased enough to try four times.

qa.q: What is Vikas planning next, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Adding a second plank at an angle, a slightly harder challenge that builds on his new balance.

qa.q: How might Karthik's parents react to the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and happy to hear about his progress, and might try a similar game at home.

grounding: A daycare teacher's pre-Christmas note records a toddler learning to steady himself on a floor plank.

passage:
Ganesh Chaturthi rain had left the field bunds muddy in Chinmay's village near Kolhapur. Santosh Ajoba held his hand as they walked to the pandal.

Chinmay pulled free. He stepped onto the narrow bund, arms wide, feet apart. He leaned left, then swung his arms and leaned right.

A frog jumped. Chinmay wobbled, dropped to one hand, caught himself, and stood again.

Santosh walked beside him, not holding on.

qa.q: What made Chinmay wobble?
qa.a: A frog jumped.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt walking on the bund by himself?
qa.a: Chinmay seemed eager and confident, pulling free to walk alone, with a moment of fright when the frog jumped.

qa.q: What did Santosh Ajoba do that helped Chinmay's balance?
qa.a: He let Chinmay walk alone but stayed right beside him, ready if needed.

qa.q: How might Santosh Ajoba feel when Chinmay caught himself?
qa.a: Santosh Ajoba was probably relieved and proud, seeing Chinmay steady himself.

grounding: A toddler practises balancing on a muddy field bund during Ganesh Chaturthi, catching himself when he wobbles.

passage:
The harmattan wind had covered Lagos in fine dust, and the yard behind the house was soft and sandy. Emeka, seven, was chasing a paper kite.

His little brother Chidi toddled after him. The sand shifted under his feet. He swayed, bent his knees, and stayed up.

Then he tried to turn quickly and sat down with a thump. He looked at Emeka, pushed up with both hands, and followed again, slower.

qa.q: What was Emeka chasing?
qa.a: Emeka was chasing a paper kite.

qa.q: How did Chidi feel after sitting down with a thump?
qa.a: Chidi seemed surprised but determined, pushing himself up and following again.

qa.q: How could Emeka help Chidi practise balance safely?
qa.a: He could run more slowly on the soft sand so Chidi can follow without turning too fast.

qa.q: How might Emeka see his little brother following him?
qa.a: Emeka might feel proud or amused that Chidi wants to keep up with him.

grounding: During the dusty harmattan season, a toddler practises staying steady on shifting sand and gets up after falling.

passage:
I'm Uma from the flat next door. On Sankranti everyone was on the terrace flying kites, and Ujjwal, who's about two, was toddling between the grown-ups.

He tried to look up at a kite and walk forward at the same time. He tilted back, stuck out one leg and caught himself. He did it again and again.

Then he bent to pick up a string, straightened slowly, and didn't fall. I couldn't tell if he was proud or just busy. He looked very serious.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal trying to do when he tilted back?
qa.a: He tried to look up at a kite and walk forward at the same time.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have been feeling as he kept catching himself?
qa.a: Uma couldn't tell, but he looked serious and focused, maybe curious or quietly proud.

qa.q: How could the adults on the terrace keep Ujjwal safe while he practises?
qa.a: Keep him away from the terrace edge and loose strings, and give him open space to toddle and look up.

qa.q: How does Uma see Ujjwal on the terrace?
qa.a: Uma watches with interest and fondness, noticing his steady progress without being sure what he feels.

grounding: A neighbour watches a toddler practise balance, shifting weight and catching himself on a crowded terrace during Sankranti.

passage:
Monday: Sabina leaned to reach her ball and tipped straight over onto the rug. Her big sister Rekha grabbed for her sleeve too late.
Thursday: Sabina squatted to pick up the ball, swayed, and flung one hand out to the sofa. She stayed up. Rekha cheered from the doorway.
The next Sunday: Sabina ran after the ball, stumbled on the rug's edge, caught herself on both hands, then stood and kept running. Rekha only looked up from her book and smiled.

qa.q: What did Sabina grab to stay up on Thursday?
qa.a: She flung one hand out to the sofa.

qa.q: What might Sabina have felt when she caught herself and kept running on Sunday?
qa.a: She probably felt confident and happy, because she stood straight up and carried on chasing the ball instead of stopping.

qa.q: How could a parent help Sabina keep building her balance?
qa.a: They could give her safe space to squat, climb low steps and chase balls, staying near without catching her every time.

qa.q: Why might Rekha react differently on Sunday than on Monday?
qa.a: By Sunday Rekha has seen Sabina catch herself, so she trusts her little sister more and no longer needs to rush over.

grounding: Shows a toddler's core strength and balance improving over several days until she can catch herself when she stumbles.
